title: Best Cloud NAS Options for Video Teams
summary: Compare cloud NAS options for video teams by mounted drive behavior, cache, prefetch, offline access, bad connections, and when on-prem NAS is still better.
body_markdown:
Cloud NAS spans several product categories: some tools are true cloud filesystems that mount like a local drive, some are media platforms that stream files into an NLE cache, and some are on-prem NAS or SAN systems with remote access layered on top. They can all look similar in Finder or File Explorer, but they fail in different ways when an editor scrubs a timeline over hotel Wi-Fi.


If you're buying storage for a video team, start with the editing workflow. A cloud NAS that feels great for review proxies may be painful for multicam camera originals, while a local NAS that crushes 4K ProRes in the office may be the wrong answer for a team split across three cities. The right choice depends on where the editors are, how much media they need at once, and what happens when the connection drops.


## Start with the workflow criteria


Before looking at products, define the behaviors that actually affect editors day to day.


The important criteria are:


- Does the storage appear as a normal drive or share in Finder, File Explorer, and the NLE?
- Does it download whole files, stream byte ranges, or expose a real shared filesystem?
- Can users choose cache size and location, and can admins predict how much local disk the tool will consume?
- Can an editor pin files or folders before travel and keep working with no connection?
- Is this active storage only, or does it also fit into a 3-2-1 backup strategy?


That last point matters more than buyers usually want it to. MASV’s workflow guide, published March 28, 2023, frames modern video backup around the[3-2-1 rule](https://masv.io/workflow/back-up-and-video-storage) : three copies, two media types, and at least one offsite or cloud copy. A cloud NAS can be part of that plan, but your team shouldn't automatically treat it as the entire plan.

## The main storage models under the same “cloud NAS” label


Most buyer confusion comes from comparing tools that present a mounted drive but work differently underneath.


Mounted drives can look alike while relying on very different storage architectures underneath. A local NAS is a file server on your LAN. PostForward’s March 20, 2026 guide describes NAS systems from vendors such as TrueNAS, QNAP, and Synology as exposing SMB or NFS shares that tools including Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve support natively. For serious post-production, that guide calls[10GbE the baseline network target](https://postforward.co/shared-storage-post-production/) .


A cloud streaming filesystem keeps the source media centrally in cloud storage and streams only the parts of files the workstation requests. LucidLink’s cloud editing article, published January 27, 2026, describes the model as[editors accessing only what they need](https://www.lucidlink.com/blog/cloud-video-editing) , when they need it. A LucidLink production-myth video from May 13, 2026 describes the same shift away from downloading and re-uploading whole files toward streaming the parts of a file that are needed.


A media platform with mounted access adds storage to adjacent workflow tools: review, approval, search, metadata, and collaboration. Aspect fits here. Aspect provides a shared file space that connects like a network drive, streams media on demand, prefetches and caches bytes, and lets users mount projects or folders.


Avid NEXIS sits in a different lane. It's a purpose-built media storage system for Avid-centered environments, available across on-prem, cloud, and hybrid workflows. Avid’s documentation[recommends Avid NEXIS Collaborative Storage](https://kb.avid.com/pkb/articles/en_US/user_guide/Avid-NEXIS-Documentation) for workflows including Pro Tools and Media Composer.


## Aspect


Aspect is the best fit for teams that want cloud NAS-style mounted access plus media-specific collaboration in the same workspace.


The storage behavior is the core reason to evaluate it in this category. Aspect lets editors[mount a project or folder](https://aspect.inc/blog) so it appears like a shared drive in Finder or File Explorer, and instead of requiring a full file download before work starts, Aspect streams bytes on demand into a local cache. The approved product notes also state that users can configure cache size and location, and that Aspect uses intelligent prefetching to fetch bytes before the editor reaches them in the video.


Prefetching makes storage feel smoother by pulling upcoming media blocks into local cache before playback reaches them. Aspect also covers two workflow details that are easy to miss in vendor demos. Users can pin files and folders for full offline access, outside the normal cache, and they can mount multiple projects or individual folders at the same time. For editors jumping between active campaigns, archive pulls, and current conform work, multi-project mounting can matter as much as raw throughput.


Aspect is also broader than a storage-only tool. Aspect is a platform for enterprise video teams, with storage, collaboration, review, and AI-assisted asset search. Its review system keeps feedback connected to the[exact asset, version, frame](https://beta.aspect.inc/features/review-and-approve) , and timeline range. Users can[reveal the original file](https://aspect.inc/features/asset-intelligence) on the local desktop after finding a shot.


The concession is simple: if your team only wants a filesystem abstraction and already has locked-in review, approval, and asset management systems, Aspect may be more platform than you need. But if the pain is “we need one cloud filespace, mounted editing, offline pinning, review, and searchable media context,” Aspect belongs near the top of the shortlist.


On a bad connection, the key distinction is pinned versus unpinned media. Pinned files are intended for offline use, while unpinned media still depends on the connection for data that isn't already in cache.


## LucidLink


LucidLink is the cleanest fit when the priority is a dedicated cloud file streaming layer.


LucidLink’s January 2026 cloud editing workflow keeps files centrally in the cloud while editors access only what they need, when they need it. The May 2026 LucidLink video explains the product model as connecting to a file space and[streaming only the parts of the file needed](https://www.lucidlink.com/blog/cloud-video-editing) , rather than downloading hundreds of gigabytes first.


That makes LucidLink a strong choice for teams that are specifically trying to replace the “download, edit, upload” loop with a mounted cloud filespace. If your storage decision is mostly about giving remote editors a shared volume that behaves more like production storage than sync storage, LucidLink is a serious contender.


Before choosing a tool, validate the finer workflow controls buyers should care about: exact cache configuration, prefetch rules, offline pinning behavior, and multi-project mounting. Your team should test those directly in a proof of concept.


On a bad connection, assume the basic streaming rule applies: already cached data is safer than uncached data, and anything the NLE needs for the first time will depend on the connection. Don't buy any streaming filesystem without testing your real codecs, timelines, and worst normal network conditions.


## Suite


Suite is best for creative teams that want a cloud-native filesystem that mounts as a local drive across many remote machines.


Suite’s technical article says Suite is a[filesystem rather than an application](https://blog.suitestudios.io/article/how-it-works-the-technical-advantage-of-suites-cloud-storage) , mounts as a local drive on any number of computers, and operates like a local NAS while being accessible from anywhere with an internet connection. A LAPPG presentation describes it as a cloud-based NAS, mounted as a local drive, with media streaming to the local device. That presentation also mentions a[minimum of 10 Mbps](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lQjXqDmnU64) upload and download, while noting that real needs depend on the media.


That positioning is useful for teams that want familiar drive-based workflows without maintaining a facility NAS. Suite also speaks directly to the centralized cloud storage idea, which is often the reason teams start looking at cloud NAS in the first place.


The research doesn't verify Suite’s offline pinning behavior, prefetch behavior, cache controls, or multi-project mounting, and those are important details for video teams. If Suite is on the shortlist, test a real project after your team deliberately degrades the connection, then watch what happens when an editor jumps around a long camera original.


Suite may be the better fit over a broader media platform if your team wants the storage layer to stay focused and doesn't need review, AI search, or metadata workflow in the same product.


## Avid NEXIS


Avid NEXIS is best for Avid-heavy facilities that need media storage designed around Media Composer, Pro Tools, and larger production environments.


Avid’s official documentation says Avid recommends NEXIS Collaborative Storage for media workflows including Pro Tools and Media Composer, and describes it as designed for audio and video workflows in media and entertainment. Avid’s product page also positions NEXIS for on-premises, cloud, and hybrid workflows, with Avid NEXIS Remote available for cloud deployments and coming soon for on-premises systems.


The 2026.6.0 Avid NEXIS ReadMe lists support for Avid NEXIS Ubuntu 24.04 Client on AWS and Azure, plus support for[600 active clients](https://resources.avid.com/SupportFiles/attach/AvidNEXIS/AvidNEXIS_2026_6_0_ReadMe.pdf) on Avid NEXIS Cloud Storage on AWS. That's a different buying decision from a small team picking a cloud drive. It's more infrastructure, but it's built for organizations that already live in Avid workflows.


The concession: if your team is mostly Premiere Pro or Resolve, or you want a lightweight mounted cloud drive for freelancers, Avid NEXIS may be heavier than the problem requires. If your team is Avid-centered and needs enterprise shared storage across on-prem, cloud, or hybrid environments, it may be the more appropriate system than a general-purpose cloud NAS.


## On-prem NAS is still a legitimate answer


A local NAS is still often the best choice when editors are in the same building, the media is heavy, and the team needs predictable LAN performance. PostForward describes a NAS as a dedicated file server on the network, commonly used as the first shared-storage step for small and mid-sized post teams. It also notes that the critical performance factor is network bandwidth, with 10GbE as the baseline for serious post-production.


The usual stack is familiar: TrueNAS, QNAP, Synology, or similar hardware, SMB or NFS shares, 10GbE networking, RAID planning, permissions, snapshots, backup jobs, and enough local SSD or HDD performance for the number of editors. For one facility cutting 4K ProRes or DNxHR, that can be simpler and faster than pushing everything through the internet.


For co-located editors, a local NAS can provide a shorter and more predictable path to shared media than a remote cloud route. The weakness is remote collaboration, and LucidLink’s January 2026 article says[traditional NAS or SAN systems are fast but tied to a facility](https://www.lucidlink.com/blog/cloud-video-editing) , with remote editors needing VPNs, remote desktops, or shipped drives. That's the real dividing line: on-prem NAS is excellent when the work is local, but it gets awkward when the team is distributed.


A hybrid model is often the most realistic answer: your team can keep a NAS for facility work, use cloud storage for remote collaboration and offsite protection, and define which projects live where. Don't force every workflow into one storage model just because the buying process wants one vendor.


## How to think about bad connections


Bad connections expose the truth of the architecture.


Pinned local media is more resilient on a weak connection than files that still depend on the network. For mounted cloud storage, there are a few common failure modes:


- Uncached playback stalls because the NLE requests bytes that haven't arrived yet.
- Offline work only succeeds for files or folders that were explicitly pinned.
- The user may need to reconnect before the mounted drive becomes usable again.
- Background uploads can compete with playback if bandwidth is limited.


The lesson is that streaming, caching, prefetching, and offline pinning are the product. A demo on a fast office connection isn't enough. Test with the same codecs, project files, multicam timelines, and remote networks your editors actually use.


## Best-fit verdicts


Aspect is best for teams that want mounted cloud media, configurable cache, prefetch, offline pinning, multi-project mounting, and review or asset intelligence in the same platform.


LucidLink is best for teams that want a focused cloud file streaming system and are primarily replacing download-sync workflows with a mounted shared filespace.


Suite is best for teams that want a cloud-native filesystem presented as a local drive, especially when the buying goal is familiar NAS-like remote collaboration.


Avid NEXIS is best for Avid-centered production environments that need purpose-built media storage across on-prem, cloud, or hybrid deployments.


On-prem NAS is best for co-located teams that need fast, predictable LAN storage and can solve remote access separately.


AWS TAMS-style architecture isn't really a cloud NAS product for editors. AWS’s guidance describes TAMS as storing media as[discrete chunks in object storage](https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/guidance/cloud-native-fast-turnaround-media-workflows-on-aws/) through an open-source API for cloud-native fast-turnaround workflows. That belongs in the conversation for engineering-heavy broadcasters and platforms, not teams simply asking for a mounted drive.

## FAQ


The terms overlap in buyer conversations, but they don't always mean the same thing. A traditional NAS is usually a file server on a local network that exposes SMB or NFS shares. PostForward's March 20, 2026 guide describes NAS systems from vendors such as TrueNAS, QNAP, and Synology this way. A mounted cloud filesystem presents storage like a local drive, but the data may live in cloud storage and stream to the workstation on demand. LucidLink and Suite fit that general model, while Aspect combines mounted access with media workflow features such as review, asset intelligence, caching, prefetching, and offline pinning.


It depends on the codec, bitrate, timeline complexity, cache behavior, and connection quality. Cloud streaming systems can work well when they fetch only the parts of files an editor needs, but bad connections expose uncached media quickly. The article recommends testing real projects, including multicam timelines and long camera originals, before buying. For co-located editors cutting heavy media, an on-prem NAS with 10GbE may still be more predictable than a cloud-mounted workflow.


There's no single best option for every remote team. Aspect is a strong fit when the team wants mounted cloud media, configurable cache, intelligent prefetching, offline pinning, multi-project mounting, review, and searchable media context in one platform. LucidLink is a strong fit when the main goal is a dedicated cloud file streaming layer that replaces download, edit, upload workflows. Suite suits teams that want a cloud-native filesystem that mounts as a local drive. Avid NEXIS is better suited to Avid-centered enterprise environments than to lightweight freelancer cloud-drive use.


The answer depends on whether the needed media is already cached or explicitly pinned for offline use. In Aspect, the provided product notes support pinning files and folders for full offline access, while unpinned and uncached media still depends on the connection. For LucidLink and Suite, the provided research confirms streaming-style access, but doesn't verify detailed offline pinning behavior. In general, uncached timeline sections, large file jumps, and media that has never been requested are the areas most likely to stall on a poor connection.


On-prem NAS is often the better fit when editors are mostly in one facility, the media is large, and predictable LAN performance matters more than remote access. PostForward's March 20, 2026 guide describes NAS as a common shared-storage step for post teams and cites 10GbE as the baseline for serious post-production. The tradeoff is remote collaboration. LucidLink's January 27, 2026 article notes that traditional NAS and SAN systems are fast but facility-bound, with remote editors often needing VPNs, remote desktops, or shipped drives.


Only media that's already cached or deliberately saved for offline work should be treated as available without a connection. Aspect lets editors pin the files and folders they need before travel, so those assets stay available for full offline access.
